title: This and that
description: Point at things with ce, cet, cette and ces, and say c’est and ce sont.

guide.summary: Ce, cet, cette and ces are the words for this, that, these and those in front of a noun: you pick the one that matches the noun. The same little word ce also builds c’est and ce sont, for saying what or who something is.

sections.title: Which word: ce, cet, cette or ces?
sections.text: French has one set of words for this and that. The choice depends on the noun that follows, never on how far away the thing is.
steps: Find the noun that follows the gap.
Plural noun: ces, for both genders.
Feminine singular: cette.
Masculine singular: ce, and cet before a vowel or a silent h.

examples.en: This week I am working a lot.

watch: The word replaces the article: ce livre, never ce le livre.
French does not choose by distance: ce livre is both this book and that book.
It agrees with the noun right after it, so check that noun’s gender, not the meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: Before a vowel: when ce becomes cet
sections.text: A masculine singular noun starting with a vowel or a silent h takes cet, so two vowel sounds never collide. The feminine cette already ends in a consonant sound, so it never changes.

rows: cet arbre, cet ami, cet été

steps: Check the gender first: a feminine noun keeps cette whatever letter follows.
For a masculine noun, say it aloud: does it start with a vowel sound?
Vowel or silent h: cet. Consonant: ce.

examples.fr: Cet été, nous partons en Italie.
examples.en: This summer we are going to Italy.

examples.fr: Je te présente cette amie, Claire.

watch: Never ce ami or ce hôtel: say them aloud and you hear why.
Cette never shortens to cet: cette amie, cette heure.
A few words have a breathed h (le héros, le hamburger); there ce stays ce.

sections.title: Plural: one word for these and those
sections.text: Every plural noun takes ces, masculine or feminine, and it covers both these and those.
steps: Look for the plural marks: an -s on the noun, a plural verb such as sont, or des nearby.
Plural: use ces and stop thinking about gender.
When you turn a sentence plural, move the verb and the adjective too: cette pomme est rouge → ces pommes sont rouges.
watch: The cet rule is only for singular nouns: ces amis, never cets amis.
One French word does the work of both these and those; -là marks those when you really need the contrast.

sections.title: Telling two things apart: -ci and -là
sections.text: Ce means this and that at the same time. To contrast two things, hang -ci (here) or -là (there) on the noun with a hyphen.
steps: Keep the normal demonstrative in front of the noun.
Put -ci on the noun for the thing near you, -là for the one further away.
Write the hyphen, and keep the accent: la with no accent is the article the.

examples.en: I prefer that dress over there.

examples.fr: Je prends ce sac-ci, pas ce sac-là.
examples.en: I am taking this bag here, not that bag there.

watch: The ending goes on the noun, not on the demonstrative: ce livre-ci, never ce-ci livre.
Use them for a contrast or a real pointing gesture; plain ce livre is usually enough.
The hyphen is not optional: cette maison-là, not cette maison là.

sections.title: c’est or ce sont?
sections.text: To say what or who something is — with un, le, mon, mes and so on — start with c’est for one and ce sont for several. Ce loses its e before est.

rows: c’est mon frère, c’est un bon restaurant
ce sont mes amis, ce sont nos voisins

steps: Look at what follows: one noun, or a plural noun?
One: c’est. Several: ce sont in written French.
Never write ces sont: ces belongs in front of a noun, not before a verb.

examples.fr: Ce sont mes amis de l’école.
examples.en: They are my friends from school.

watch: In speech many people say c’est mes amis; written French keeps ce sont.
Before mon, un or le + noun, use c’est, not il est: c’est mon frère.
Il est and elle est go with an adjective or a job with no article: il est français, elle est médecin.

sections.title: ce, se, ces, ses: same sound, different job
sections.text: These pairs sound identical, so the ear cannot help you. What decides is the word that follows: a noun or a verb.

rows: il se réveille, elle se lève

steps: Look at the word right after the gap.
A verb follows: it is se (s’ before a vowel).
A noun follows: choose between the pointing words (ce, cet, cette, ces) and the owner word (ses).
Ask the meaning: are you pointing at it, or saying whose it is?

examples.fr: Il se réveille à sept heures.

watch: Ces nuages means those clouds; ses nuages would mean his clouds.
Se never stands before a noun, and ce never stands before a verb.
Ce sont has no -s on ce; se sont belongs to a past tense: ils se sont levés.

steps: Find the noun after the gap and ask: masculine or feminine?
Check it is singular: no -s, and a singular verb.
Take that row of the table and put the word straight in front of the noun.
Check the gender first: a feminine noun keeps its one form whatever letter follows.
For a masculine noun, say the noun aloud and listen to the first sound.
A vowel or a silent h at the start needs the longer masculine spelling; a consonant takes the short one.
Look for plural marks: an -s on the noun, or a plural verb.
A plural noun takes one demonstrative for both genders, so gender no longer matters.
If you are rewriting, make the verb and the adjective plural as well.
Keep in front of the noun the demonstrative that matches it.
Decide which thing is near the speaker and which is further away.
Attach the ending to the noun with a hyphen, and check its accent.
Look at the noun after the gap: one, or several?
Use the singular form for one and the plural form for several in written French.
Keep ces for the front of a noun: it never stands before the verb sont.
Look at the word right after the gap: is it a verb or a noun?
A verb needs the reflexive pronoun; a noun needs a pointing word or an owner word.
For a noun, ask the meaning: pointing at it, or saying whose it is?
Then check singular or plural to pick the spelling.

exercises.hint: Pantalon is one masculine thing.
exercises.feedback: Match the gender and number of pantalon.
exercises.explanation: Pantalon is masculine singular and starts with a consonant, so this is ce.

mistakes.why: Cette is the feminine form. Pantalon is a masculine noun (un pantalon), so the feminine word does not agree with it.
Ces is the plural form, for several things. Un pantalon is one item, and it has no -s here.

exercises.hint: Chanson is feminine.
exercises.feedback: Match the gender of chanson.
exercises.explanation: Chanson is feminine singular, so this song is cette chanson.

mistakes.why: Ce goes with a masculine noun. Chanson is feminine (la chanson), so it needs the feminine demonstrative.
Cet is a masculine form, used only before a vowel. Chanson is feminine and starts with a consonant.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for this.
exercises.source: Je voudrais ____ gâteau, s’il vous plaît.
exercises.hint: Gâteau is masculine and starts with a consonant.
exercises.feedback: Use the plain masculine form.
exercises.explanation: Gâteau is masculine singular and starts with a consonant, so this cake is ce gâteau.

mistakes.why: Cette is for feminine nouns. Gâteau is masculine (le gâteau), so it takes the masculine form.
Cet is the masculine form used before a vowel or a silent h. Gâteau begins with the consonant g.
Ces is plural. You are asking for one cake, so the noun is singular.
Le is the article the; it does not point at anything. The English says this, so a demonstrative is needed.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for this.
exercises.hint: Semaine is feminine.
exercises.feedback: Use the feminine form.
exercises.explanation: Semaine is feminine singular, so this week is cette semaine.

mistakes.why: Ce is the masculine form. Semaine is feminine (la semaine), so the demonstrative must be feminine too.
Cet is a masculine form used before a vowel. Semaine is feminine, and s is a consonant anyway.
Ces is plural. The sentence is about one week, the one you are in.
La is the article the. La semaine does not point at this particular week.

exercises.source: Ce voiture est à mon père.
answers: Cette voiture est à mon père.
exercises.hint: What is the gender of voiture?
exercises.feedback: Ce only goes with masculine nouns.
exercises.explanation: Voiture is feminine singular, so this car is cette voiture.

answers: Ce voiture est à mon père.
mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged, and its first word is exactly the error: voiture is feminine (la voiture), so a masculine demonstrative cannot stand in front of it.

answers: Cet voiture est à mon père.
mistakes.why: Cet is another masculine form, used only before a vowel sound. Voiture is feminine and starts with v.

answers: Ces voitures sont à mon père.
mistakes.why: That turns one car into several. Only the word in front of voiture is wrong; the number of the sentence was fine.

exercises.hint: Sac is masculine.
exercises.feedback: Match this to the gender of sac.
exercises.explanation: Sac is masculine singular and starts with a consonant, so this bag is ce sac.

mistakes.why: Cette is feminine. Sac is masculine (le sac), so the demonstrative does not agree with it.
That says these bags are heavy. The English has one bag, so noun, verb and adjective all stay singular.
The final -e makes the adjective feminine. It describes sac, which is masculine, so it keeps its plain form.
Se is the pronoun that goes before a reflexive verb (il se lave). Before a noun the pointing word starts with c.

exercises.instruction: Replace siège with place and change the demonstrative to match. Write the whole sentence.
exercises.hint: Place is feminine.
exercises.feedback: The demonstrative must follow the new noun.
exercises.explanation: Place is feminine singular, so ce becomes cette.

mistakes.why: You changed the noun but left the masculine demonstrative. Place is feminine (la place), so the word in front of it has to change too.
You changed the demonstrative but kept siège. The instruction asks you to put place in, and the demonstrative follows that new noun.
Cet is a masculine form used before a vowel. Place is feminine and starts with a consonant.
Nothing has changed: the noun is still siège, and the sentence was not asked to keep it.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: This cheese is very good. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.hint: Fromage is masculine.
exercises.feedback: Match the demonstrative to fromage.
exercises.explanation: Fromage is masculine singular and starts with a consonant, so this cheese is ce fromage.

mistakes.why: Fromage is masculine (le fromage), so the feminine tile does not agree with it.
Très strengthens the adjective, so it stands right before bon, not before the verb.

exercises.hint: How many flowers?
exercises.feedback: Fleurs is plural.
exercises.explanation: Fleurs is plural, so these flowers is ces fleurs.

mistakes.why: Cette is singular, for one feminine thing. Fleurs ends in -s and the verb is sont: there are several flowers.
Ce is singular and masculine. Fleurs is plural, and fleur is a feminine noun anyway.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for these.
exercises.hint: Chaussures is plural.
exercises.feedback: Plural nouns have one form for this and these, whatever the gender.
exercises.explanation: Chaussures is plural, so these shoes is ces chaussures.

mistakes.why: Cette is singular. Chaussures ends in -s: you are talking about a pair of shoes, several things.
Ce is the masculine singular form. Chaussures is plural, and it is feminine too.
Cet is a masculine singular form used before a vowel. Number comes first here, and chaussures is plural.
Ses means his or her. The instruction asks for these, which points at the shoes rather than naming their owner.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for those.
exercises.hint: Enfants is plural.
exercises.feedback: The vowel rule for cet is only for singular nouns.
exercises.explanation: Enfants is plural, so those children is ces enfants. French uses the same word for these and those.

mistakes.why: Cet is a singular form, used before a vowel. Enfants is plural, so the vowel rule does not apply at all.
Cette is singular and feminine. The verb sont and the -s of enfants both show there are several children.
Ce is singular. Qui sont tells you the sentence is about more than one child.
Ses means his or her children. The question points at the children in front of you instead.

exercises.instruction: Make enfant plural and change the rest of the sentence to match.
exercises.hint: The plural demonstrative has one form.
exercises.feedback: Change the demonstrative, the noun, the verb and the adjective.
exercises.explanation: Plural enfants takes ces, with sont and sages.

mistakes.why: Only the first word moved to the plural. Making enfant plural means the noun, the verb and the adjective all follow.
Cet is a singular form; it cannot stand in front of a plural noun.
Cette is singular and feminine, so it matches neither the number nor the gender of enfants here.
The subject is now several children, so the verb and the adjective have to become plural as well.
That is the sentence unchanged: the noun is still one single child.

exercises.instruction: Make pomme plural and change the rest of the sentence to match.
exercises.hint: The plural demonstrative has one form for both genders.
exercises.feedback: Change the demonstrative, the noun, the verb and the adjective.
exercises.explanation: Plural pommes takes ces, with sont and rouges.

mistakes.why: Only the first word became plural. The noun, the verb and the adjective have to follow it.
Cette is a singular form; it cannot stand in front of a plural noun.
The subject is now several apples, so the verb and the adjective need their plural forms.
The adjective agrees with what it describes: with several apples it takes an -s too.
That is the sentence unchanged: pomme is still singular.

exercises.hint: Apartments is plural.
exercises.feedback: Check the demonstrative for a plural noun.
exercises.explanation: Appartements is plural, so these apartments is ces appartements.

mistakes.why: Cet is a singular form used before a vowel. Appartements is plural, so the singular form cannot go with it.
Cette is singular and feminine. Appartement is masculine, and here there are several of them.
The adjective agrees with the noun: several apartments means an -s on it as well.
Ses means his or her apartments. The English says these, which points at them instead.

exercises.hint: The h of hôtel is silent.
exercises.feedback: Hôtel is masculine and sounds as if it starts with a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Hôtel is masculine singular with a silent h, so ce becomes cet: cet hôtel.

mistakes.why: Ce is the plain masculine form, but it never stands before a vowel sound. The h of hôtel is silent, so the word begins with an o sound.
Cette is feminine. Hôtel is masculine (un hôtel), whatever letter it starts with.

exercises.hint: Homme starts with a silent h.
exercises.feedback: Ce cannot stand right before a vowel sound.
exercises.explanation: Homme is masculine singular with a silent h, so that man is cet homme.

mistakes.why: Ce cannot stand right before a vowel sound, and the h of homme is silent, so two vowels would collide.
Cette is the feminine form. Homme is masculine (un homme).

exercises.hint: Arbre is masculine and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Ce cannot stand right before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Arbre is masculine singular and starts with a vowel, so this tree is cet arbre.

mistakes.why: Ce never stands directly before a vowel, and arbre begins with a.
Ces is plural. Arbre has no -s here: it is one tree.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for this.
exercises.hint: Été is masculine and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Think of the form used before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Été is masculine singular and starts with a vowel, so this summer is cet été.

mistakes.why: Ce is the masculine form used before a consonant. Été begins with a vowel, so the masculine form takes its longer spelling.
Cette is feminine. L’été is masculine, so the feminine form does not fit even though the noun starts with a vowel.
Ces is plural. You are talking about one summer, the coming one.

exercises.instruction: Write the French word for that.
exercises.hint: Acteur is masculine and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Think of the form used before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Acteur is masculine singular and starts with a vowel, so that actor is cet acteur.

mistakes.why: Ce is not used before a vowel sound, and acteur starts with a.
Cette is feminine. Un acteur is a man, so the noun is masculine; a woman would be une actrice.
Ces is plural. The question is about one actor.

exercises.hint: Say ce ami aloud: two vowels collide.
exercises.feedback: Ami starts with a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Ami is masculine singular and starts with a vowel, so this friend is cet ami.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged, and its first two words are the problem: two vowel sounds cannot meet like that in French.
Cette is feminine. Ami with no -e is a male friend, so the noun is masculine.
That makes it several friends. The sentence talks about one friend; only the word in front of ami has to change.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: This hospital is new. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.hint: The h of hôpital is silent.
exercises.feedback: Look at the first sound of hôpital.
exercises.explanation: Hôpital is masculine singular with a silent h, so this hospital is cet hôpital.

mistakes.why: The h of hôpital is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound and the short masculine tile cannot stand in front of it.

exercises.hint: Enfant is masculine here and starts with a vowel.
exercises.feedback: Check the demonstrative before a vowel.
exercises.explanation: Enfant for a boy is masculine singular and starts with a vowel, so that child is cet enfant.

mistakes.why: Enfant begins with a vowel, and the short masculine form is never used before one.
Cette is feminine. The brackets say the child is a boy, so the noun is masculine here.
The final -e makes the adjective feminine. The child is a boy, so the adjective keeps its plain form.
That is several children. The English points at one child, so everything stays singular.

exercises.hint: Amie is feminine. Does the feminine form need to change before a vowel?
exercises.feedback: Cet is only for masculine nouns.
exercises.explanation: Amie is feminine singular, so this friend is cette amie. Cet is only for masculine nouns; cette already ends in a consonant sound, so it never changes.

mistakes.why: Cet is a masculine form. Amie with an -e is a woman — Claire — so the noun is feminine, and the feminine form needs no special spelling before a vowel.
Ce is masculine as well, and it never stands before a vowel. Amie is feminine here.

exercises.instruction: Write the ending that means there.
exercises.source: Je préfère ce livre-ci, pas ce livre-____.
exercises.hint: -ci means here; the other ending means there.
exercises.feedback: Check the accent: without it the word means the.
exercises.explanation: Ce livre-ci is this book here; ce livre-là is that book there. Là needs its accent.

mistakes.why: That is the article la (the), with no accent. The ending that means there carries an accent, and the two are different words.
-ci marks the thing nearest you, and the first book already has it. The second one is the other book, further away.
Ce is the pointing word that goes before the noun, and it is already there. The gap is the small ending after the hyphen.

exercises.instruction: Choose the ending that means there.
exercises.source: Tu préfères cette robe-ci ou cette robe-____ ?
exercises.hint: The two dresses are in different places.
exercises.feedback: Look closely at the accent.
exercises.explanation: Cette robe-ci is this dress here, cette robe-là is that dress there. Là with an accent means there.

mistakes.why: La with no accent is the article the. It does not mean there, and it cannot hang on a noun with a hyphen.
-ci points at what is near the speaker, and the first dress already carries it. The second dress is the other one.

exercises.source: This shirt (here) is blue and that shirt (there) is white.
answers: Cette chemise-ci est bleue et cette chemise-là est blanche.
Cette chemise-ci est bleue et celle-là est blanche.
exercises.hint: Chemise is feminine; add -ci for here and -là for there.
exercises.feedback: Put -ci and -là on the noun with a hyphen.
exercises.explanation: Cette chemise-ci points to the shirt here and cette chemise-là to the one there.

answers: Cette chemise-ci est bleue et cette chemise-la est blanche.
mistakes.why: The second ending has lost its accent, which turns it into the article la.

answers: Cette chemise-là est bleue et cette chemise-ci est blanche.
mistakes.why: The two endings are swapped: the shirt marked (here) is the near one and the shirt marked (there) is the far one.

answers: Ce chemise-ci est bleu et ce chemise-là est blanc.
mistakes.why: Chemise is feminine (la chemise), so both the demonstratives and the colour adjectives need feminine forms.

answers: Cette chemise ci est bleue et cette chemise là est blanche.
mistakes.why: Both endings are floating as separate words. They are joined to the noun with a hyphen.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: I take this bag here, not that bag there. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.source: I take this bag here, not that bag there.
answers: Je prends ce sac-ci, pas ce sac-là.
exercises.hint: Here is -ci, there is -là.
exercises.feedback: Sac is masculine and starts with a consonant.
exercises.explanation: Ce sac-ci is the bag here and ce sac-là the bag there.

answers: Je prends cet sac-ci, pas ce sac-là.
Je prends ce sac-ci, pas cet sac-là.
mistakes.why: Cet is used only before a vowel or a silent h, and sac begins with the consonant s.

exercises.instruction: Add -là to the noun to point at the house over there.
exercises.hint: Join the ending to the noun with a hyphen.
exercises.feedback: Add the ending for there to maison.
exercises.explanation: Cette maison-là means that house there.

mistakes.why: Nothing has been added: the sentence still just says look at that house, without pointing over there.
Without its accent, la is the article the, so the ending no longer means anything after the hyphen.
-ci points at what is near the speaker. The house you are told to point at is over there, further away.
The ending is not a separate word: it hangs on the noun with a hyphen.

exercises.hint: Look at the last word.
exercises.feedback: La without an accent means the.
exercises.explanation: The ending that means there is -là, with an accent.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Its last word is the article la: the accent is missing.
-ci means here, near the speaker. That changes what the sentence points at instead of fixing the spelling.
Dropping the hyphen does not fix it: the ending belongs to the noun, and it still needs its accent.

exercises.hint: Amis is plural.
exercises.feedback: Check the spelling of each word, too.
exercises.explanation: Before a plural noun, written French uses ce sont.

mistakes.why: Ces is the pointing word you put in front of a noun (ces amis); it is never the subject of a verb.
Se sont belongs to a reflexive verb in the past, as in ils se sont levés. Here you are simply saying who these people are.

exercises.hint: One person.
exercises.feedback: Look at the spelling and the number.
exercises.explanation: For one person introduced with a word like ma, use c’est.

mistakes.why: Ce sont is the plural form, used before a plural noun. Ma grand-mère is one person.
S’est belongs to a reflexive verb in the past, as in elle s’est levée. It cannot introduce a noun.

alternatives.message: In speech people say c’est nos voisins, but written French uses ce sont before a plural noun.

exercises.hint: Voisins is plural.
exercises.feedback: Written French uses a plural verb here.
exercises.explanation: Nos voisins is plural, so written French uses ce sont.

mistakes.why: Ces goes straight in front of a noun (ces voisins). It never stands before the verb sont.
Se sont is part of a reflexive past tense (ils se sont vus), not a way of saying who people are.
Ils sont names people already identified. To say who someone is with nos, mes or un, French starts with the little word ce.

exercises.hint: One restaurant.
exercises.feedback: The noun is singular.
exercises.explanation: Un bon restaurant is singular, so it is c’est.

mistakes.why: Ce sont goes before a plural noun. Un bon restaurant is one restaurant.
Ces is a pointing word for a plural noun, and it never comes before the verb.
Il est goes with an adjective or a job with no article (il est français). Before un + noun French uses the pointing form.
Ce loses its e before a vowel, so these two words are written as one with an apostrophe.

alternatives.message: Before a word like mon, un or le + noun, French uses c’est, not il est: c’est mon frère.

exercises.hint: Use the form for pointing at one person.
exercises.feedback: Before mon + noun, French does not use il est.
exercises.explanation: To say who someone is with a word like mon, use c’est: c’est mon frère.

mistakes.why: Ce sont is for several people, and mon frère is one person.
S’est belongs to a reflexive past tense (il s’est levé); it is not a way to introduce someone.
Frère is masculine (le frère), so the possessive in front of it must be masculine too.

alternatives.message: That is common in speech, but written French uses ce sont before a plural noun.
Before a word like mes + noun, French uses ce sont, not ils sont.

exercises.hint: Parents is plural, and you are saying who they are.
exercises.feedback: Before mes + noun, French does not use ils sont.
exercises.explanation: To say who several people are, written French uses ce sont: ce sont mes parents.

mistakes.why: Ces is the pointing word used in front of a noun (ces parents), never before the verb.
Se sont belongs to a reflexive past tense (ils se sont vus), not to saying who people are.
Mon is singular. Parents is plural, so the possessive has to be plural as well.
The noun keeps its -s: there are two of them, so parents stays plural.

exercises.instruction: Make cousin plural and change the rest of the sentence to match.

alternatives.message: That is common in speech, but written French uses ce sont before a plural noun.

exercises.hint: The plural of c’est changes two words.
exercises.feedback: Change c’est, the possessive and the noun.
exercises.explanation: A plural noun takes ce sont in written French: ce sont mes cousins.

mistakes.why: Nothing has changed: cousin is still singular, and so are the two words in front of it.
The verb has become plural but the possessive and the noun have not followed it.
Ces belongs in front of a noun (ces cousins); before the verb, the word has no -s.
Making cousin plural means putting an -s on the noun too, not only on the words in front of it.

exercises.hint: The first word is not the one that means these.
exercises.feedback: Before sont, use the word ce with no s.
exercises.explanation: The expression is ce sont; ces means these and goes before a noun.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Ces is the word you put in front of a noun (ces livres), so it cannot be the subject of sont.
That is what people say out loud, but written French uses the plural verb before a plural noun like mes livres.
Se sont is part of a reflexive past tense (ils se sont vus); it does not introduce a noun.

exercises.hint: The gap is before a verb.
exercises.feedback: Ce points at a thing; this word goes with a verb.
exercises.explanation: Se réveiller is a reflexive verb, so it is il se réveille. Ce only goes before a noun.

mistakes.why: Ce points at a noun (ce matin). Réveille is a verb, and a reflexive verb takes its pronoun right in front of it.
Ces is the plural pointing word and goes before a plural noun. The next word here is a verb.

exercises.hint: Here the word means this, before a noun.
exercises.feedback: This word points at matin.
exercises.explanation: Ce matin means this morning; se only goes before a verb.

mistakes.why: Se only sits in front of a verb, as in il se lève. Matin is a noun.
Ses means his or her and goes before a plural noun (ses livres). Matin is singular, and nobody owns the morning.

exercises.hint: The meaning is his, not these.
exercises.feedback: One of these words points, the other shows the owner.
exercises.explanation: Ses shows the owner (his books); ces would mean these books.

mistakes.why: Ces means these or those: it points at the books instead of saying they belong to Paul.
Ce is singular and goes before a masculine singular noun. Livres is plural, and the meaning asked for is his.

exercises.hint: The meaning is these, not his.
exercises.feedback: One of these words points, the other shows the owner.
exercises.explanation: Ces points at the clouds: ces nuages. Ses would mean his or her clouds.

mistakes.why: Ses means his or her clouds, which makes no sense here: nobody owns the sky. The question points at them.
Se is the pronoun of a reflexive verb (il se lave). Nuages is a noun, so this word cannot go with it.

exercises.hint: The gap is before a verb.
exercises.feedback: Ce goes before a noun; look at the next word.
exercises.explanation: Se promener is a reflexive verb: elle se promène.

mistakes.why: Ce goes in front of a noun (ce chien). Promène is a verb, so it needs its reflexive pronoun.
Ces is the plural pointing word and stands before a plural noun, never before a verb.
Ses means his or her and goes before a noun. What follows the gap is the verb promener.

exercises.instruction: Write ces or ses. The meaning is these.
exercises.hint: You are pointing, not saying whose.
exercises.feedback: The word for these starts with c.
exercises.explanation: Ces couleurs means these colours; ses couleurs would mean his or her colours.

mistakes.why: Ses means his or her colours. The instruction says the meaning is these, so you are pointing, not naming an owner.
Se only goes before a verb (il se lave). Couleurs is a noun.
Cette is singular and feminine, but couleurs is plural, and one plural form covers both genders.

exercises.hint: Restaurant is a noun, not a verb.
exercises.feedback: The first word sounds right but is spelled wrong.
exercises.explanation: Before a noun, this is ce; se only goes before a verb.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged. Se can only stand in front of a verb, and restaurant is a noun.
Ses means his or her and goes with a plural noun. Nobody owns the restaurant here, and it is singular.
Ces is plural, but restaurant has no -s and the verb is est: the sentence is about one restaurant.

exercises.instruction: Fix the error. Marie loves her own parents.
exercises.hint: The meaning is her parents.
exercises.feedback: The word you need shows the owner.
exercises.explanation: Ses shows the owner (her parents); ces means these.

mistakes.why: That is the sentence unchanged: ces parents means those parents over there, not the ones who are hers.
Ce is singular, so it cannot go with a plural noun, and it still points instead of naming the owner.
Se is the pronoun of a reflexive verb (elle se lève); it never stands before a noun.
Son is for a singular noun. Parents is plural, so the possessive must be plural too.

exercises.instruction: Build the sentence: She gets up early. Leave one tile unused.
exercises.hint: Se lever is a reflexive verb.
exercises.feedback: The word before the verb is not the one that points at things.
exercises.explanation: Se lever is reflexive, so it is elle se lève. Ce would point at a noun.

mistakes.why: Ce goes before a noun, never before a verb. Lever is reflexive here, so the verb needs its own pronoun.
